paper_title: What Matters for Latent Reasoning with Flow Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Latent reasoning lets a large language model (LLM) think in a continuous space and verbalize only the answer. We argue that an effective latent thought must meet five requirements: it should be useful, helping produce the correct answer rather than merely changing it, diverse, so that resampling yields different reasoning trajectories, explainable, so that a decoded chain of thought (CoT) reflects reasoning the answer actually follows, refinable with more inference compute, and efficient, costing less than an explicit CoT at comparable accuracy. Current methods rarely meet these requirements: they learn shortcuts from the question, distill the explicit CoT into their weights, or imitate it one token at a time. We focus on flow matching in a learned latent space, the family we argue is best placed to meet them, and identify the training choices that make it work. The result is Flow-based Latent Reasoning (FLaRe), a simple recipe covering what the latent space encodes and how to shape it, where to train the flow, how to read out the answer, and a final stage of training on the model's own verified thoughts. A probe for each requirement shows that FLaRe improves on prior latent methods in all five. It also compares favorably with them on arithmetic benchmarks, while reaching 97% of the accuracy of explicit CoT at a quarter of its latency.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on test-time scaling (Snell et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025), reasoning at length before producing final answer. This reasoning is usually written as an explicit chain of thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022), generated autoregressively one token at time. While effective, explicit CoT has three limitations. Its cost grows with the length of the chain, much of this cost is spent on prose that adds little to the reasoning (Hao et al., 2025), and single rollout commits to its early tokens, so exploring another path requires further generation. Latent reasoning targets these limitations by carrying the intermediate computation in continuous states and verbalizing only the answer. In principle, sampling from distribution of latent thoughts can explore different trajectories without generating every intermediate step in words, and thus be more efficient. Existing latent methods differ in how they replace the token-by-token computation of explicit CoT. Horizontal methods feed continuous representations back one slot at time (Hao et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025), while vertical methods reason within hidden states or by looping block of layers (Deng et al., 2023, 2024; Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025). Parallel methods refine block of slots together through fixed-point iterations (Wu et al., 2025; Kuzina et al., 2026) or by denoising in learned latent space for reasoning (Kang et al., 2026) or text planning (Lovelace et al., 2025). In this work, we argue that an effective latent thought must meet five requirements: it should be useful, diverse, explainable, refinable and efficient. We focus on flow matching in learned latent space, as in latent diffusion models (Lovelace et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2026), since it offers direct route to four of them. Different noise draws yield different thoughts, decoder reads each thought back as an explicit CoT, more denoising steps give thought more compute, and small code costs less to generate than an explicit CoT. As for usefulness, it depends on the methods design choices, which must ensure that the answer relies on the thought. Concretely, latent flow matching starts by training variational autoencoder (VAE) to compress CoTs into latent space. Conditioned on the question, flow model then refines Gaussian noise into latent thought in this space, from which the same model generates the final answer autoregressively. In practice, with standard text diffusion, this pipeline falls far behind explicit CoT, and it works only when few training choices are made right. We present these choices as simple recipe, Flow-based Latent Reasoning (FLaRe), that follows the 1 Figure 1 Flow-based Latent Reasoning (FLaRe). (a) VAE encodes symbolic CoT rsym into small code z, corrupted in training for smooth latent space, and its decoder reads it back as rsym or, given the question q, as natural language CoT rlang. (b) In stage 1, the shared flow model θ learns to denoise the code given the question and to answer from its own thought ˆz. (c) In stage 2, on new questions with answers only, θ proposes thoughts per question, and those whose decoded answer is correct are re-encoded as flow targets. The model is updated with the flow loss on these targets and an answer loss Lroll backpropagated through the full denoising path. pipeline from the latent space to the last stage of training  (Fig. 1)  . The VAE, trained with dual reconstruction objective, encodes symbolic CoT, stripped of its wording, into small code that fine-tuned decoder reads back both as the symbolic CoT and, given the question, as its natural language counterpart. Its latent space is shaped by corrupting the inputs and codes in training rather than by tightening reconstruction. The flow is trained mostly near pure noise, where inference starts, and with several CoTs per question. Its answer reader is trained on the flows own predicted thoughts as well as on noised codes, so that it learns to read imperfect thoughts as generated at test time. Finally, short stage 2 self-trains the model on its own verified rollouts for new questions, generating thoughts from pure noise as at inference and backpropagating the answer loss through the full rollout. Our main contributions are: simple training recipe. Through controlled ablations, we identify the training choices that make latent flow matching work for reasoning, from learning the latent space to self-training on verified rollouts, and combine them into FLaRe. Requirements for latent reasoning, and probes for them. We define five requirements an effective latent thought must meet, that it be useful, diverse, explainable, refinable and efficient, design probe for each, and show that FLaRe improves on prior latent methods in all five. Improved accuracy and efficiency. FLaRe compares favorably with prior latent methods on arithmetic benchmarks and reaches 97% of explicit CoT accuracy at quarter of its latency.

sections.title: 2.1 Explicit and Latent Reasoning
sections.content: First, we provide the relevant background and key concepts of reasoning with LLMs. Given question q, model with parameters θ produces reasoning variable pθ(r q), followed by an answer pθ(a q, r). Explicit and latent reasoning differ in the form of r. Explicit CoT. With explicit CoT (Wei et al., 2022), = (c1, . . . , cL) is sequence of vocabulary tokens generated autoregressively, pθ(r q) = QL l=1 pθ(cl q, c<l). We study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on dataset = {(q, r, a)} of questions q, explicit CoTs and answers a. This explicit CoT training dataset will also be used to train our latent reasoning model. Latent reasoning. Here stays in continuous space and is never verbalized during thinking. Vertical methods reason within the models hidden states without separate thought. Horizontal and parallel methods, including 2 ours, instead use latent thought = = (z1, . . . , zM ) RM of slots of dimension d, with pθ(z q). Horizontal methods produce the slots one at time, while parallel methods refine all of them together. After thinking, the answer is generated token by token from the question and the latent thought, pθ(a q, z).

sections.title: 2.2 Latent Reasoning with Flow Matching
sections.content: In this paper, we learn the latent thought RM via flow matching in learned latent space, as in latent diffusion (Lovelace et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2026), in two steps. First, VAE (Kingma and Welling, 2014) is trained on the explicit CoT dataset to encode each CoT into compressed latent code. Then, flow model (Lipman et al., 2023) is trained to generate these latent codes conditioned on the question (Kang et al., 2026). At inference, the same shared flow model thinks by denoising, refining Gaussian noise into latent thought, then produces the final answer autoregressively. Architecture. The VAE encoder, the VAE decoder and the shared flow model θ, which generates both the latent thought and the answer, are all LLMs (Kang et al., 2026). VAE training. Both the encoder and the decoder are initialized from base LLM with parameters ϕ and ψ, respectively. The encoder reads [r Z1 ZM ], an explicit CoT followed by learned slot tokens. Its final hidden states at the slot positions give the mean and log-variance of the posterior qϕ(z r) = ϕ(r)(cid:1), from which the code is sampled as = µϕ(r) + σϕ(r) ϵ with ϵ (0, I). The decoder (cid:0)µϕ(r), diag σ2 reads [z AE], where AE is learned marker, and reconstructs from the code alone. The encoder and decoder minimize the β-VAE objective (Higgins et al., 2017): LVAE = Eqϕ(zr) (cid:2) log pψ(r z)(cid:3) + β DKL (cid:0)qϕ(z r) (0, I)(cid:1), (1) where β weights the KL term. After training, the flow targets are the posterior means, standardized per slot and dimension as = (µϕ(r) m)/s (Meshchaninov et al., 2025). Flow matching. After VAE training, each example becomes (q, z, a). For [0, 1], we interpolate from Gaussian noise ϵ (0, I) at = 0 to the clean VAE code at = 1: zt = (1 t)ϵ + tz. The flow model learns the constant velocity ϵ along this path (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Li and He, 2026). The shared model θ reads [q SOT zt EOT SOA a], where SOT and EOT bracket the thought, embeds time, and SOA starts the answer (Kang et al., 2026). In the flow pass, the slots attend bidirectionally, and their final hidden states are projected to dimension to predict velocity under the flow matching loss as follows: LFM = E(q,z), t, ϵ h(cid:13) (cid:13)vθ(zt, t, q) (z ϵ)(cid:13) 2 (cid:13) 2 , (2) where is drawn from distribution over [0, 1] that sets which noise levels receive most of the training signal. We average the loss over four independent (t, ϵ) draws per code, as in MAR (Li et al., 2024), to reduce gradient variance and speed convergence. During flow training, the question is replaced by null token with probability 0.1 to enable classifier-free guidance (CFG) at inference (Ho and Salimans, 2022). After the flow pass, the same training step runs an answer pass, which in its base form reads the clean VAE code at = 1 and minimizes LCE = log pθ(a q, z). The joint objective is = λFMLFM + LCE, with λFM weighting the flow loss. Inference. Given question q, we start from Gaussian noise z0 = ϵ and run Euler steps from = 0 to = 1 with guidance scale w. The resulting latent thought ˆz = z1 serves as the reasoning variable, and the same shared model generates the answer pθ(a q, ˆz) autoregressively. These steps replace the generation of an explicit CoT, while different noise draws can yield different thoughts for the same question. The frozen VAE decoder renders ˆz as an explicit CoT for offline analysis and for checking decoded final answers against references during stage 2.

The decoded reading checks whether the model thinks correctly, that is, whether its thought solves the question, while the direct reading checks whether the model can then use this thought to answer. The decoded reading is also more forgiving, because the decoder generates the CoT token by token and can turn latent near valid code into well-formed CoT, so it still relies on explicit CoT generation. The direct reading has no such correction and tests how cleanly the thought lands in the VAE space. The gap between the readings thus measures the mismatch between generated thoughts and clean VAE codes that the decoder hides. thought that decodes to wrong answer typically fails both readings, while one that decodes to the correct answer can still be misread and fail the direct one.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Reconstruction Alone Is Not Sufficient
sections.content: High VAE reconstruction does not by itself produce codes that the flow can generate accurately. At = 512, increasing the code from 8 to 32 slots raises reconstruction from 96.8% to 99.4% but lowers direct accuracy from 47.1% to 25.4% and decoded accuracy from 53.2% to 32.3% (Tab. 1). Across 66 VAEs from nine sweeps that vary the capacity, corruption, objective, encoder, decoder and training data, reconstruction and decoded accuracy have correlation of 0.12  (Fig. 2)  , and several of the best-reconstructing VAEs are among the worst downstream. Higher reconstruction thus makes the code more precise but harder to generate. At inference, the flow must build from the question alone complete thought that solves the problem and remains decodable, so every detail the code preserves is one more detail to generate. 3.1.2 Smoothness Is Necessary generated thought rarely matches clean VAE code exactly. Nearby codes should therefore decode consistently, and the decoder must tolerate approximate thoughts. Reconstruction and the KL term of equation 1 do not ensure this, and increasing β degrades reconstruction before it improves generation. We thus keep β = 105 and corrupt both the encoder input and latent code during VAE training. Each input CoT token is replaced by random token with probability psub = 0.3, while the decoder target stays clean. Half of the sampled codes 1 δ2ξ, with ξ (0, I) and δ = 0.7. We also apply latent receive variance-preserving noise, δz + dropout with probability pdrop = 0.4 (Meshchaninov et al., 2025). All three corruptions improve direct accuracy relative to removing any one of them. Token substitution has the largest effect on decoded accuracy (Tab. 2). Compared with no corruption, they improve both readings despite lower reconstruction. The corruptions thus do the opposite of added capacity: each CoT is encoded as smooth region rather than precise point, so thought that lands nearby still decodes to it, and the flow only has to reach the region. Without them, neighboring codes decode to different CoTs, so thought that lands near the right code keeps the plan but may be decoded to different values. 3.1.3 The Target Must Be Information Dense To see which style of CoT better fits latent reasoning with flow matching, we pair each question in our training data with two CoTs: symbolic CoT rsym that only records the reasoning steps and intermediate results needed to reach the answer, and its paired natural language CoT rlang that explains the same steps in plain language  (Fig. 3)  . The training set is thus Dvae = {(q, rsym, rlang, a)}. The encoder then reads either CoT, and the decoder writes CoT back through one of two routes. The symbolic route writes rsym from the code alone, [z AE], so the code must carry every reasoning step. The language route writes rlang, and with symbolic input it also reads the question, [z AE] with learned marker Q, which supplies the entities, units and wording that the symbolic CoT omits. Training both routes, which we call the 5 dual routes, gives the following dual reconstruction objective: LVAE = Eqϕ(zrsym) (cid:2) log pψ(rsym z) log pψ(rlang z, q)(cid:3) + β DKL (cid:0)qϕ(z rsym) (0, I)(cid:1). (3) VAE with single route keeps only its own reconstruction term. In Tab. 3 we compare four VAEs with different inputs and decoder routes. The results show that the symbolic CoT is the better input and VAE that encodes the natural language CoT loses about 10 direct and 17 decoded points against the default. The symbolic CoT is also far more compressible, since the same eight slots reconstruct nearly every held-out symbolic CoT exactly but fewer than half of the natural language ones. Training the decoder on the dual routes also helps in two ways. First, the second reconstruction regularizes the code for more effective flow matching, and second, it yields single frozen decoder that renders latent thought as either symbolic or natural language CoT, which we use to probe the model. We therefore take the symbolic CoT as input and the dual routes as our default. For datasets with only natural language CoTs, we propose to convert each CoT with an LLM that, given the symbolic language and its rules, segments the CoT into elementary steps and compiles each step into its symbolic form (Appendix D). 3.1.4 Stronger Decoder Improves Downstream Accuracy With the 1B encoder fixed, fine-tuned 3B decoder gives the strongest result among the decoder sizes and training choices in Tab. 1. One possible explanation is that it lets the encoder omit details the decoder can recover, giving the flow an easier target. It may also read approximate generated thoughts more robustly. The Final Recipe. We carry forward an 8 512 VAE with symbolic CoTs as encoder input, dual decoder routes, all three corruptions, 1B encoder, and fine-tuned 3B decoder. Tab. 10 lists its hyperparameters.

sections.title: 3.2 The Flow Matching
sections.content: The flow model is trained on Dflow = {(q, z, a)}, where cached VAE codes replace the explicit CoTs of Dvae. Its training objective is = λFMLFM + LCE, as defined in Sec. 2.2, with λFM = 5. We study four choices: where along the path to train, what the answer pass reads, which training data to use, and whether to train end to end through the full rollout. 3.2.1 The Flow Is Trained Mostly Near Noise The flow loss of equation 2 regresses velocity at sampled time t, whose distribution determines which parts of the path receive most of the training. Our sweeps vary only this distribution, comparing uniform time with logit-normals (Esser et al., 2024) shifted increasingly toward noise  (Fig. 4)  . Uniform time performs worst, and the model learns well only when training is strongly shifted toward noise, where inference starts. Otherwise, it mainly learns to refine nearly intact codes. The required shift grows with latent dimension (Esser et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026), since larger codes retain more information at the same noise level. sections.title: 3.2.2 The Answer Pass Must Read Imperfect Thoughts
sections.content: In each training iteration, second forward pass through the same model places latent code zans at the slot positions at time = 1 and predicts the answer tokens with the cross-entropy loss LCE = log pθ(a q, zans). Tab. 4 compares five settings. Exact code reads the VAE code z, while noised code reads it lightly pulled toward noise. Predicted only reads the flows one-step endpoint ˆz = zt + (1 t) vθ(zt, t, q), computed with the guided velocity vθ used at inference and detached from the flow. The two mixture settings read 50/50 split of predicted endpoints and noised codes, either detaching the endpoints or allowing the answer loss to train the flow through them. The direct reading results in Tab. 4 show that training on the models own predictions is necessary. Since generated thoughts differ from VAE codes, reader trained on exact or noised codes alone misreads them, and mixing predictions with noised codes 50/50 works best. However, these predictions must stay detached, since they are noisy one-step estimates of the code, and backpropagating the answer loss through them conflicts with the flow loss. The new questions are the GSM8K-like and MATH-like questions of OMI-2, whose natural language CoTs we convert into symbolic ones (Appendix D). Tab. 5 shows that several CoTs per question give the largest gain in both readings, while new questions help less and questions of different style lower accuracy. With one CoT per question, different noise draws still yield different thoughts, but each question is paired with single target code, and diffusion models trained on few samples per condition tend to memorize them (Gu et al., 2025; Kadkhodaie et al., 2024). With several CoTs, each question has several modes, and the flow must map different noise draws to different valid solutions rather than to one code. Diverse training data is thus necessary for latent reasoning with flow matching, as it teaches the flow to cover the space of all valid solutions rather than single one. 3.2.4 End-to-End Training through the Full Rollout Is Required After stage 1, the decoded reading remains several points above the direct one. The generated thoughts therefore often contain the correct answer, but the models readout is not adapted to them. Two limitations keep stage 1 from closing this gap. First, the answer pass trains on mixture of noised codes and detached one-step endpoints, while inference builds thoughts from pure noise over guided steps, whose errors differ from those seen in training. Second, the answer loss updates the shared backbone but does not train thought generation through the flow steps. This stage uses only new questions and their reference answers, without requiring additional CoT annotations, learned reward or reinforcement learning objective. For each block of new questions, the EMA model generates = 8 thoughts per question from centered noise over = 20 guided steps. The frozen VAE decoder reads each thought into symbolic CoT, and all distinct CoTs whose final answer matches the reference are retained. The retained CoTs are re-encoded into latent codes for the next round of training updates. Each update combines the flow loss on these codes and stage 1 replay with an answer loss on fresh rollout from noise over = 10 guided steps. The answer loss backpropagates through every step and both guidance branches. This teaches the reader to use generated thoughts and the flow to produce thoughts that yield the reference answer. The updated EMA model then generates thoughts for the next block. Tab. 6 examines each part of this loop with the parent model, VAE, question pool and schedule held fixed. These gains come from the answer loss through the full rollout, since removing it, detaching the rollout endpoint or reducing the rollout to single step loses most or all of them. sections.title: 4 Analysis: The Requirements of Latent Reasoning
sections.content: Effective latent reasoning requires thoughts that are useful, helping produce the correct answer, and diverse, so that resampling can explore different reasoning trajectories for the same question. These trajectories should also be explainable, with recovered CoTs that reflect the reasoning the answer actually follows. At inference, the thoughts should remain refinable with more compute and efficient, costing less than explicit CoT at comparable accuracy. With our final recipe fixed, we examine these requirements through targeted probes, comparing FLaRe with Coconut, CODI and PCCoT, with explicit CoT as reference. Tab. 7 summarizes the results, with details in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4.1 Useful Latent Thoughts
sections.content: A latent thought should carry question-specific computation that helps produce the correct answer. For Coconut and CODI, prior work reports little change in accuracy when thoughts are removed, especially on logical reasoning tasks (Rizvi-Martel et al., 2026; Dilgren and Wiegreffe, 2026), or, for Coconut, swapped across questions (Zhang et al., 2025a). Training by curriculum or distillation can internalize the CoT in the models weights, allowing shortcut from the question to the answer (Zhang et al., 2025a; Cui et al., 2026; Aswal et al., 2026). We probe this dependence with twin test: changing one number in question produces twin with different answer. We inject the models thought for the twin into the original question and measure how often the answer matches the twins answer. Explicit CoT follows the twins CoT on 97% of pairs, compared with 40% and 37% for our two stages, 32% for CODI, 28% for PCCoT and 7% for Coconut (Tab. 7). The harder twins often produce incorrect thoughts. Among pairs that each model answers correctly on both questions before injection, our following rates rise to 91% in stage 1 and 76% in stage 2. Zeroing the thought or giving the reader only the question also reduces accuracy in both stages, supporting the thoughts contribution to correct answers (Appendix E.1).

sections.title: 4.2 Diverse Latent Thoughts
sections.content: Resampling should explore different valid trajectories for the same question, providing coverage that voting, verification, reinforcement learning or self-training can turn into higher accuracy. Coconut, CODI and PCCoT generate single thought deterministically, and the superposition Coconut was designed for collapses after finetuning (Rizvi-Martel et al., 2026). New candidates therefore require perturbing the thought at inference (Wang et al., 2026b,a). We probe this diversity with sampling test of 16 thoughts per question, using independent noise draws for our flow and noise perturbations for the baselines. We measure coverage as pass@16, the share of questions solved by at least one sample, and test whether majority voting improves on the greedy answer. The baselines gain at most 5 points of coverage, and voting never improves on greedy. On the decoded reading, our stage 1 model gains 16.6 points of coverage and 3.3 through voting, while stage 2 gains 14.7 and 1.8, respectively. Stage 2 retains most of this coverage while improving single-sample accuracy (Appendix E.2).

sections.title: 4.3 Explainable Latent Thoughts
sections.content: An explainable latent thought should decode into an explicit CoT that reflects the reasoning the answer follows. The baselines lack dedicated thought decoder, so their thoughts are read through the LM head, since thought fed back as an embedding often behaves like its nearest token (Rizvi-Martel et al., 2026). This recovers only fragments (Shen et al., 2025), and full trajectories require an explicit search over candidate traces (Dilgren and Wiegreffe, 2026), which still does not show that the answer follows them (Aswal et al., 2026). We probe recovery with reading test that checks whether every reference intermediate result appears in order, in the top-1 LM-head tokens for the baselines and as complete values in the CoT decoded by the frozen VAE decoder for ours. Our thoughts meet this criterion on about half of the questions, more often than any baseline (Tab. 7). We then probe faithfulness on twin pairs whose edit changes an intermediate value. Our decoded thoughts usually recover the twins value, and the answer follows this recovered reasoning far more often than for the baselines (Appendix E.3).

sections.title: 4.4 Refinable Latent Thoughts
sections.content: More inference compute should refine latent thought until accuracy saturates, as in test-time scaling of explicit CoT (Snell et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025). Existing methods are constrained by their training budgets: Coconut becomes unstable beyond two thoughts per reasoning step (Hao et al., 2025), CODI peaks at six latent tokens (Shen et al., 2025), and PCCoT at three Jacobi iterations (Wu et al., 2025). We probe this with budget sweep of each frozen model, including budgets beyond those used in training. In Tab. 7, raising the budget from tenth to half that of explicit CoT adds at most 6.1 points to the baselines, and PCCoT even loses accuracy, while our decoded reading gains 18.2 and 24.2 points in stages 1 and 2 and the direct reading gains at most 1.8. Since the flow is trained across noise levels, more Euler steps keep refining its thought, while the baselines peak at or below their training budgets (Appendix E.4). 9 Table 8 Direct answer accuracy (%) of models trained on GSM8K-Aug, on GSM8K (IID) and on GSM8K-Hard, SVAMP and MultiArith (OOD). sections.title: 4.5 Efficient Latent Thoughts
sections.content: Since latent reasoning does not verbalize every step, it should cost less than explicit CoT at comparable accuracy. We probe this trade-off with latency test of accuracy and time to answer on one GPU, one question at time. In Tab. 7, the best baselines reach 94% of explicit CoT accuracy at 2.0 speedup (CODI) or 91% at 3.9 (PCCoT), while our stage 2 model, with the direct reading at two Euler steps, reaches 97% at 3.9 (Appendix E.5).

sections.title: 5 Comparison with Prior Latent Reasoning Methods
sections.content: Following CODI and KaVa, Tab. 8 reports direct accuracy on GSM8K and zero-shot transfer to GSM8KHard (Gao et al., 2023), SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021) and MultiArith (Roy and Roth, 2015). FLaRe follows the final recipe of Sec. 3.2, whose Diverse CoT and stage 2 questions help adapt the LLM to flow matching, task it was not pretrained for, while all other methods except LaDiR build on its autoregressive abilities. Even stage 1, trained on the same GSM8K-Aug and Diverse CoT rows as LaDiR, our most direct competitor, which also denoises in learned latent space, gains 10.7 to 21.0 points on GSM8K, so the gap comes from the design choices of Sec. 3 rather than from the data. Stage 2 then improves every column at every scale, by 2.7 to 3.8 points on GSM8K. It leads all latent methods on GSM8K at 0.5B and 1B, by 6.9 and 2.6 points over KaVa, performs comparably to it at 3B, and leads or ties on GSM8K-Hard at every scale. SVAMP is the main exception, likely because nearly half of its questions add distractor numbers, which are rare in GSM8K-Aug.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Tab. 9 first places each method on the design axes of the paper: the family, where the thought lives, how it is produced, what supervises it, whether it can be decoded and how, and whether the inference budget is fixed at training or adjustable. Earlier methods keep the thought in the models embeddings or hidden states, produce it one slot at time or through fixed number of iterations, learn it from an explicit CoT teacher, and read it, if at all, through the LM head at budget fixed at training. The diffusion family and ours generate the thought in learned latent space by denoising, with an adjustable budget, and decode it through the VAE decoder. Latent reasoning. Latent reasoning methods (Chen et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025b) move the intermediate computation of explicit CoT (Wei et al., 2022) from discrete tokens into an implicit hidden computation, conducted either vertically over fixed set of input slots, within the hidden states (Deng et al., 2023) or by looping (Saunshi et al., 2025), or horizontally with added tokens or blocks of tokens, without generating an intermediate text sequence at inference. 10 Table 9 Latent reasoning methods along the design axes of the paper. The first family transfers the thinking from explicit next tokens into the hidden states (Deng et al., 2023, 2024; Yu et al., 2024), as models already perform some multi-hop reasoning latently (Yang et al., 2024b; Biran et al., 2024; Lindsey et al., 2025). Filler tokens. Pause or filler tokens appended between the input and the answer (Goyal et al., 2024; Pfau et al., 2024), or after each word in recurrent language models (Herel and Mikolov, 2024), widen the parallel computation before the answer without adding sequential feedback steps, akin to register tokens in vision Transformers (Darcet et al., 2024). Continuous feedback. Autoregressive feedback methods, popularized by Coconut (Hao et al., 2025), keep the mechanism of explicit CoT but feed the continuous representation of each step back as the next input instead of discrete token, as in CODI (Shen et al., 2025) among others (Cheng and Van Durme, 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Tan et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026). These methods are analyzed theoretically by Zhu et al. (2025a). Looped computation. Looped or recurrent methods (Dehghani et al., 2019; Giannou et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025c) keep the number of slots fixed and apply the same layers over them several times, so the reasoning becomes an iterative computation within the hidden states (Wang et al., 2025; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Baek et al., 2026). Newer methods loop over fixed block of slots in parallel instead of one step at time, as in PCCoT (Wu et al., 2025) and KaVa (Kuzina et al., 2026). Whatever their use of computation, most of these methods still use the explicit CoT in training, through curriculum as in Coconut and stepwise internalization (Deng et al., 2024), or distillation (Deng et al., 2023) as in CODI and KaVa. Diffusion. Latent diffusion models for text (Lovelace et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Meshchaninov et al., 2025) generate by denoising latent variable from Gaussian noise. In reasoning and planning, the latent is denoised, conditioned on the input, into state that encodes step or the full trajectory, followed by autoregressive generation, as in LaDiR (Kang et al., 2026) and Lovelace et al. (2025), with the latent space induced by VAE trained on explicit CoT (Kang et al., 2026).

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we studied what matters for latent reasoning with flow matching through controlled ablations of every stage of the pipeline, and distilled the answers into simple recipe. We then set out five requirements latent reasoning method should meet, useful, diverse, explainable, refinable and efficient, designed probe for each, and found that the thoughts of FLaRe improve on those of prior latent methods in all five. FLaRe also compares favorably with them on arithmetic benchmarks, while reaching 97% of the accuracy of explicit CoT at quarter of its latency.

A.4 Variable-Length Latent Thoughts fixed width asks one code to hold both one-step and long CoT, while explicit CoT spends more tokens on harder questions. Our recipe supports latent thought of variable width with almost no change, and unlike LaDiR (Kang et al., 2026), which varies the length by generating one block after another, the thought stays single block of slots refined in parallel and only gets wider or narrower. This keeps the method as efficient as with fixed width since the number of sequential passes stays 2S whatever the width, whereas block-wise generation repeats the whole denoising for every block. The VAE registers the largest number of slot tokens and uses the first of them, the flow model generates slots with the loss of equation 2 averaged over the active slots, and can be chosen at inference. Two designs. The VAE has 16 slot tokens and encodes each CoT with 8, 12 or 16 of them, chosen by the length of the CoT: 8 up to 16 encoder tokens, 12 up to 24, and 16 beyond. In quarter of the cases one of the two other widths is used instead, so that every width is trained on CoTs of every length, and the flow model is trained on the same mix of widths. The two designs differ in how the codes of different widths relate. In the nested design, each slot token attends only to the slots before it, so the first 8 slots of 16-slot code are exactly the 8-slot code, and one encoder pass at 16 slots gives all three widths, as in Matryoshka representations (Rippel et al., 2014; Kusupati et al., 2022) and nested tokenizers (Bachmann et al., 2025). In the elastic design, the slot tokens attend to each other in both directions, so each width has its own code, computed by separate encoder pass per width, as in elastic tokenizers (Yan et al., 2025). Outcome on GSM8K-Aug. The nested design trains and generates at every width as intended, but on GSM8KAug it brings no gain since 8 slots already suffice. The symbolic CoTs are short, with median of 21 encoder tokens and 90% below 35 tokens. Eight slots already reconstruct 98.7% of the test CoTs exactly, and increasing the number of slots to 16 adds only 0.4 points. The extra slots therefore carry little, weak residual of the first eight at about half their scale. As result, the best variable-width model only matches the fixed width of 8 (60.1 decoded for both), and choosing the width by the length of the CoT does not beat it. While variable widths do not help on this dataset, we expect them to on data whose CoTs vary more in length, since the recipe is flexible and applies to variable widths with almost no change. In that case, the width becomes thinking budget chosen at inference (Muennighoff et al., 2025; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025). VAE. Each symbolic step takes the place of sentence and is encoded into its own block, code of three slots of dimension 512 (so that, averaged over the dataset, CoT takes about as many slots as our fixed 8). In the last block we include an answer-only suffix so that stopping head can learn when the CoT is complete. The encoder and decoder (Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.2-3B) start from the OMI-2 language VAE that also initializes ours, and the encoder is fine-tuned, on single steps, with the objective of equation 1, with token substitution and additive Gaussian latent noise. In stage 1 it predicts the velocity of each noised block given the clean preceding blocks, with uniform time and bidirectional attention within each block, and the answer and stopping losses read the clean codes. Stage 2 keeps the same supervised rows but replaces the preceding blocks with blocks generated by 10-step guided rollouts, with gradients through the rollout. The flow, answer and stopping losses are weighted 5, 1 and 2, and the optimizer is that of our recipe (Tab. 10). Inference. Blocks are generated sequentially until the stopping head fires or 16 blocks have been generated, using guidance = 4 and noise scale 2. The answer is then sampled at temperature 0.7. As for our model, each block takes 20 Euler steps, and stage 1 is read with the EMA weights and stage 2 with the LIVE weights. Efficiency comparison. LaDiR generates one block per reasoning step, and each block needs full denoising of guided steps, as much as our whole thought. Its cost therefore grows with the length of the reasoning. GSM8K test CoTs have 3.3 steps on average and 5 at the 90th percentile, so at 20 steps LaDiR runs about 130 sequential forward passes per question, against 40 for our model. At our measured 22 ms per guided Euler step, this is about 1.5 per question on average and 2.2 at the 90th percentile, against 0.46 for our direct reading, or 3.2 to 4.8 times slower than our model and 5.5 times slower than explicit CoT. The gap widens with fewer steps. LaDiR needs 10 to 20 Euler steps per block, since its answer is not trained on the models own one-step 17 endpoints and each block builds on the previously generated ones, whose errors accumulate. Our answer pass is trained to read such endpoints in stage 1, and our direct reading reaches 57.4 after only two steps, in 68 ms, 11 to 21 times faster than LaDiR at 10 to 20 steps per block.

sections.title: D Symbolic Conversion Pipeline
sections.content: This pipeline turns dataset with natural language CoTs into the paired format of Dvae. The symbolic language. The converter targets small-step language that includes GSM8K-Aug arithmetic as subset. Each CoT consists of BODY markers in ASCII mathematics, with one move per marker: an equation, an inequality, declaration in R, definition u_1:=3*4, or guarded case. Every name must come from the question or an earlier declaration, and the final marker contains only the answer. Converter. Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), sampled at temperature 1 with its highest reasoning effort and fixed seed per row, is given the language and its rules, the question, the CoT split into numbered sentences, and the reference answer. It returns groups of elementary symbolic steps, each naming the sentences it compiles, or rejects the CoT, or flags the question as ill-posed, and the natural language CoT is never rewritten. Run on OMI-2. Before conversion, filter keeps 2M of the 13M rows of OMI-2. It rejects rows with false equation or conclusion that contradicts the label, keeps CoTs under 256 tokens with explicit reasoning and no backtracking, removes the questions of all GSM8K-Aug sets, and keeps at most eight distinct solutions per question. blind audit, in which the converter answers each question alone, then keeps the 57.5% of the questions whose answer matches the label. The converter succeeds on 96.3% of the remaining rows, and review in fresh context, which sees the question, the original CoT and the symbolic one together, accepts 90.5% of the 700,131 distinct traces. After deduplication and final leakage check, 629,824 pairs over 119,835 questions remain. Examples. Tab. 15 shows two published pairs, one IID and one OOD. Future directions. While we provide this conversion as simple offline LLM-based step, the converter could also be trained with execution feedback by writing symbolic CoTs as executable programs (Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), and the symbolic structure could even be induced directly in the latent space from task feedback alone (Macfarlane et al., 2026). We leave both directions for future work. The Requirements of Latent Reasoning: Details All probes use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fine-tuned on GSM8K-Aug and, unless noted, the 1,319 GSM8K test questions. The baselines are the released checkpoints of CODI (Shen et al., 2025) and PCCoT (Wu et al., 2025), and those of Coconut, explicit CoT and No-CoT from Dilgren and Wiegreffe (2026), whose reported accuracies we reproduce within half point. E.1 Useful: The Twin Test Probe. The twin test asks whether the answer comes from the thought or from the question alone. Each test question gets twin that changes one number, and we obtain the twins CoT and answer by recomputing the reference CoT with the new number. For example, the twin of If Ann is 9 years old and her brother is twice her age, how old will her brother be in 3 years? makes Ann 8, so the CoT 9*2=18 18+3=21 becomes 8*2=16 16+3=19 and the answer changes from 21 to 19. We first run the model on the twin and keep its thought, then run it on the original question with this thought in place of its own. The question now leads to 21 and the thought to 19: the answer follows the thought if it is 19, keeps the question if it is 21, and is neither otherwise. The injected thought is the twins recomputed CoT for explicit CoT, and for ours the thought that the flow generates for the twin from the same noise draw.
